extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of literary criticism; readers learning close reading of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for close-reading and judging emotional effects, sentimentality, and doctrinal content in poems; explains what counts as appropriate emotion, how sentiments differ from emotions, and how poetic assumptions operate emotionally and intellectually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crude versus refined emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: A crude emotion is aroused by a wide manner of situations; a refined emotion can only be aroused by a narrow range of situations. Crudeness and refinement are qualitative, not quantitative characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refined responses can be more appropriate but more likely to go astray; crude emotions are less likely to be entirely wrong but less likely to be entirely right. Neither crudeness nor refinement necessarily implies intensity (e.g., violent emotions are usually crude). Judge poems for the qualitative character of the emotion rather than raw intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity (violence) of emotion ≠ value
rubrics_metrics.description: Violence of emotion does not necessarily imply value; 'the quality rather than the violence which matters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems which are very 'moving' may nevertheless be negligible or bad; evaluate the quality and appropriateness of the feeling, not merely how much it moves the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sentiment (psychological)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentiment is not a momentary experience but a more or less permanent arrangement in the mind: a group of tendencies towards certain thoughts and emotions organised around a central object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentiments persist and are formed through past experience; they can include complex tendencies (e.g., love contains resentful tendencies). When evaluating a poem, distinguish transient emotions from underlying sentiments that may shape responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality defined (third sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: A response is sentimental when, either through the over-persistence of tendencies or through the interaction of sentiments, it is inappropriate to the situation that calls it forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inappropriateness usually occurs by (a) confining to one aspect of the situation, or (b) substituting a factitious, illusory situation that may have little in common with the real one. Extreme cases appear in dreams and asylums. Use this operational definition when deciding whether a response or poem is 'sentimental'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish authorial sentimentality from reader susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When calling a poem 'sentimental' one may mean either (1) that the poem is the product of a mind too easily stirred (the author is sentimental) or (2) that we ourselves would be too easily moved (the reader is sentimental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate these two claims; sometimes only the second applies. Compare evidence (e.g., signs of facile expression) before attributing sentimentality to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete, near, coherent situation to justify emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether the situation as given is concrete enough, near enough, and coherent enough to justify the vigorous emotional response invited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's business is to present the situation (often through the same words as the emotion). If certain effects are aimed at, certain methods (nearness, concreteness, coherence) are thereby prescribed. Close reading is required to determine whether these qualities are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion must be properly founded in the presented situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotion is justified only if it is founded in the specifics of the situation presented by the poem rather than an abstracted theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An abstract theme (e.g., 'a girl bewailing her lover') cannot alone justify extreme sympathetic emotion; the particulars of the speaker, diction, cadence, movements of thought and feeling are part of the situation and must support the emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on conventional/borrrowed decorations
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional metaphors and borrowed decorations often fail in nearness and concreteness and are frequently irrelevant to the central impulse of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such elements tend not to hang together and produce incoherence; their combined effect is likely to be crude and to invite undirected, objectless feeling. Evaluate whether figurative language is integral to the situation or merely reach-me-down ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence of imagery and items
rubrics_metrics.description: The various items and decorations in a poem should 'hang together' — i.e., form a coherent whole relevant to the central impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incoherent pooling of images (e.g., conflicting seasonal imagery) indicates weakness of central impulse and supports charges of sentimentality; coherence is a test of whether emotional responses are controlled and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine what response is invited as well as the presented situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deciding whether a poem is sentimental in a given sense, be sure you know both what the presented situation is and what response is invited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the very closest reading will tell enough about either to make judgment worthwhile; many mistaken accusations arise from misreading the situation or misunderstanding the intended response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimental fixations often stem from inhibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most sentimental fixations and distortions of feeling are the result of inhibitions (avoidance of painful aspects of life), producing narrowed, specialised, or displaced emotional responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether sentimental emphasis masks avoidance of other aspects; note social and historical patterns of inhibition (e.g., attitudes to tears). Recognise that inhibition is sometimes necessary, but permanent curtailment of possibilities is pathological for poetic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosis and cure: expansion rather than destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: The safe cure for mawkish attachment to an illusory sentiment is to take the distorted sentiment and work it into close and living relation with some scene concretely and truthfully realised (treatment by expansion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to cure by sneers, realism, or drying-up responses are ineffective and may impoverish emotional life. Evaluate whether the poet enlarges and integrates sentimental elements or merely suppresses them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish poetic 'assumptions' emotionally vs intellectually
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'assumption' in poetry may be entertained either intellectually (as a proposition in a logical context) or emotionally (in a context of sentiments, feelings and tendencies to action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which mode dominates: intellectual assumption requires logical support; emotional assumption functions as a device to elicit emotional belief. This distinction matters for whether a poem's doctrinal content can be read by dissenting readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the poem require doctrinal belief for full imaginative realisation?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the statements or doctrines presented in a poem are merely poetic fictions or whether actual belief in them seems required for full and perfect imaginative realisation (i.e., whether doctrinal dissent is a real obstacle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the poem's emotional force seems to invite assent, note that some readers may be compelled emotionally toward the doctrine; evaluate whether the work nevertheless remains accessible to dissenting readers or whether it depends on the reader's adoption of poet's beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification of emotional belief: prudence and non-interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional belief is justified by its success in meeting our needs (prudence), not by logical relations; poetry can enable emotional belief without interfering with the intellectual system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a poem's doctrinal or belief-like elements, ask whether their emotional appeal is prudent (serves needs) and whether poetry prevents those emotional beliefs from disruptive interference with the reader's intellectual convictions.
